of
something. In this lesson you learn to read a numeral in

base, to write any number in
any base, to move between bases, to count how many digits a number needs, and to solve the GATE
puzzles where the base itself is the unknown. By the end, a question like "for which base
?" will be a two-minute calculation, not a guess.

This is the first lesson of Digital Logic, and almost everything later leans on it. Binary,
octal and hexadecimal (next lesson) are just bases 2, 8 and 16. Fractions and fixed point
(Lesson 3) extend place value to the right of the point. Signed numbers (Lesson 4) reuse the
same digits with one place given a negative weight. Later chapters read counter states, memory
addresses and IEEE-754 fields with exactly the tools built here.

The idea: a digit counts bundles

attrs.title: Digits count bundles, positions name the bundle size

c:
Think of a shop that only uses bundles of three: loose items, packets of 3, boxes of 3 packets
(9 items), crates of 3 boxes (27 items). To record 46 items you fill crates first: one crate
(27), then two boxes (18), no packets, and one loose item. The record reads

Each position holds the number of bundles of one size, and the sizes grow by the same factor
(here 3) as you move left. A position can never hold 3 or more, because three of anything
would be packed into one bundle of the next size. That one rule, "pack as soon as you reach
the base", is all of positional notation. Our everyday decimal is the same shop with bundles
of ten.

An odometer is the same shop in motion. Watch a counter whose wheels only know the digits 0, 1
and 2: when a wheel would reach 3 it rolls back to 0 and nudges its neighbour forward.
Notice what the counter shows after three counts:

. In base 3, "10" means one bundle of
three and nothing loose, which is three. That is why "10" means

in every base:
ten in decimal, two in binary, sixteen in hexadecimal.

, optionally followed by a radix point and
more digits
Digits ten to thirty-five are written A to Z, so in hexadecimal A = 10, B = 11, …, F = 15.

Here is that definition doing its work: the same four digits, first read in base 3 and then
in base 5. Only the place values change.

horner-chain.title: Horner's chain: (257)₈ to decimal
horner-chain.intro: Start with a running total of 0. Each arrow will multiply the total by the base 8 and add one digit.

elements.text: Horner's chain for (257)₈: multiply by 8, add the next digit

steps.caption: Take the running total 0, multiply by 8 and add the next digit 2: 0 × 8 + 2 = 2.
Take the running total 2, multiply by 8 and add the next digit 5: 2 × 8 + 5 = 21.
Take the running total 21, multiply by 8 and add the next digit 7: 21 × 8 + 7 = 175.
Every digit has been used, so the last total is the value: (257)₈ = 175. The same total comes from 2·64 + 5·8 + 7, but without writing any powers.

odometer-rollover.title: An odometer that rolls over at 3
odometer-rollover.intro: Four counter wheels, all at 0. Under each wheel is the place value it stands for: 27, 9, 3 and 1.

elements.text: A base-3 counter (each wheel shows 0, 1 or 2)

steps.caption: One count: the right wheel moves from 0 to 1.
Two counts: the right wheel shows 2, the largest digit base 3 allows.
Three counts: the right wheel cannot show 3, so it rolls back to 0 and pushes the next wheel on by one. The display reads 10, which in base 3 means one three and no ones.
Jump ahead to 26 counts: every wheel shows its largest digit, 222. That is 2·9 + 2·3 + 2 = 26 = 3³ − 1.
One more count makes every wheel roll over in turn, and the carry ripples to a new wheel: 1000 in base 3 is 3³ = 27. In any base, 1 followed by k zeros is b to the power k.

place-value-strip.title: Place value: the same digits in base 3 and base 5
place-value-strip.intro: The digits 1 2 0 1 in four cells. Above each cell is its place value in base 3, a power of 3 that grows from right to left.

steps.caption: The first digit is 1 and sits in the 3³ = 27 place, so it adds 1 × 27 = 27. Running total: 27.
The second digit is 2 and sits in the 3² = 9 place, so it adds 2 × 9 = 18. Running total: 45.
The third digit is 0 and sits in the 3¹ = 3 place, so it adds 0 × 3 = 0. Running total: 45.
The fourth digit is 1 and sits in the 3⁰ = 1 place, so it adds 1 × 1 = 1. Running total: 46. So (1201)₃ = 46.
Now keep the same four digits but switch the base to 5. Only the place values change: 125, 25, 5 and 1.
Weighting each digit again: 125 + 50 + 0 + 1 = 176. Same digits, larger base, larger value: (1201)₅ = 176.

radix-solutions-grid.title: Counting radix solutions: every candidate pair, with the invalid ones explained
radix-solutions-grid.intro: Two tables of candidate pairs. A tick marks a pair that satisfies the equation and every digit limit. A cross names the rule the pair breaks: y = 1 is not a base, the digit 8 needs y ≥ 9, and the digit 4 needs x ≥ 5.

repeated-division-ladder.title: Repeated division: 2748 to hexadecimal
repeated-division-ladder.intro: We will divide by 16 again and again. Each remainder becomes one hex digit.

elements.text: Convert 2748 to base 16: divide by 16, keep the remainder

steps.caption: Divide 2748 by 16: quotient 171, remainder 12, which is written C in hex. This first remainder is the units digit.
Divide 171 by 16: quotient 10, remainder 11, which is written B in hex. Carry on with the quotient.
Divide 10 by 16: quotient 0, remainder 10, which is written A in hex. The quotient is now 0, so we stop.
The first remainder is the lowest digit and the last remainder is the leading digit, so read the column from the bottom up: A, B, C.
